summaries.A0053:
State-regulated legalisation shows that strict cannabis regulation can reduce the harmful effects associated with prohibition while producing tangible social and economic benefits.

Although imperfect, the Canadian and Uruguayan models demonstrate that state-regulated legalisation works by providing an effective framework for reducing cannabis-related crime, improving consumer safety and generating revenue for essential public programmes. These results far exceed those of strict prohibition.
summaries.A0054:
Canada's state-regulated legalisation demonstrates that strict cannabis regulation works better than prohibition.

* '''Description:''' Full legalisation with strict regulation (minimum age, advertising restrictions, production controls and state distribution).
* '''Examples:''' Canada and some US states.
* '''Advantages:'''
** A substantial reduction in the black market.
** High tax revenues to fund public programmes.
** Control over product quality and the varieties available.
* '''Disadvantages:'''
** The need for substantial legislative and administrative infrastructure.
** Some consumers continue buying on the black market because legal prices are high.
* '''Results:'''
** '''Canada:''' A smaller black market and better product quality, although youth consumption remains a challenge.
** '''Overall assessment:''' The best model for a nationwide approach, but one that requires constant monitoring and adjustment.
summaries.A0056: According to the mayor of Windsor, a city on the Canada–US border, legalising cannabis in Canada could cause “longer delays at the border” and disrupt cross-border trade.
summaries.A0057:
The cannabis industry will promote mass consumption at the expense of public health.

Legalising cannabis creates a market dependent on continued, excessive consumption, similar to the tobacco and alcohol markets, with economic interests that run counter to public health.

summaries.A0063: By legalising cannabis, the state can impose strict production and distribution standards, ensuring that no toxic or dangerous substances are added to the product. This protects consumers from the risks associated with adulterants used on the black market, such as solvents or heavy metals.

summaries.A0102:
Uruguay's state-regulated legalisation demonstrates that strict cannabis regulation works better than prohibition.

* '''Description:''' Legalisation with state control over production and distribution. Only residents may buy cannabis, and quantity limits apply.
* '''Advantages:'''
** Almost complete elimination of the black market.
** State control over quality and prices.
** Tax revenue to fund prevention programmes.
* '''Disadvantages:'''
** Heavy bureaucracy and restrictions that can put users off.
** Difficulty persuading consumers accustomed to the black market.
* '''Results:'''
** A substantial reduction in the black market, but a slight increase in overall consumption.
** '''Overall assessment:''' A viable model that works better than strict prohibition, with scope for adjustment.

quote_texts.Q104: If some people eat quantities of food that damage their health, we do not look for the cause of that behaviour in the food, but in their reasons for eating compulsively. […] Similarly, if some people use illicit drugs to the point where they can no longer manage their lives, we should question not the drugs themselves but those people's reasons for using them in that way.
quote_texts.Q105: Addiction is an illness, but one whose determinants are social long before they are physical. Uncontrolled gambling, like alcoholism and drug addiction in many cases, feeds on the anxiety about tomorrow that now afflicts most workers and very many young people. Prevention that tackles the roots of the problem requires profound social change: society must be put back on its feet and made to work first and foremost for humanity.
quote_texts.Q106: One of the most persistent beliefs used to justify retaining the prison system is that imprisonment guarantees our safety. This implies that the people locked up are mainly those who have committed “violence against persons”. Yet a large majority of prisoners are held for offences relating to the use or trade of illicit substances, which puts the idea that “all prisoners are violent” into perspective.
quote_texts.Q107: Who are these prisoners? Three quarters are in pre-trial detention. The others have problems that owe more to mental ill health or socioeconomic deprivation than to criminality. “Prisoners who are purely a matter for the Criminal Code account for only 10%,” the management stresses: people who are genuinely dangerous and must be isolated from the rest of society.
quote_texts.Q108: Society has the right to do everything it can to reduce the situations for which it will have to bear the cost.
quote_texts.Q109: Combating cannabis is just as legitimate as combating tuberculosis.
quote_texts.Q111: Cannabis intoxication causes around 300 road deaths each year, as the 2005 SAM study (Drugs and Fatal Road Traffic Accidents) revealed. Yet that study took account only of blood THC concentrations above 2 micrograms per litre (μg/L), whereas we can now measure THC at a concentration ten times lower (0.2 μg/L). Combining cannabis and alcohol multiplies the risk of a fatal accident by fourteen. Reducing road accidents requires the eradication of cannabis and stricter measures on alcohol.
quote_texts.Q112: The serious harms caused by drug addiction to human beings, both as individuals and as citizens, and to society as a whole have been demonstrated. Article 5 of the 1789 Declaration allows the law to prohibit “actions harmful to society”: drug use is certainly one such action.
quote_texts.Q113: Drugs are not merely a public health problem; they are also a threat to democracy.
quote_texts.Q114: Expanding the range of legal drugs would mean much greater lethality, with a major deterioration in collective intelligence into the bargain.
quote_texts.Q115:
Adding cannabis to tobacco increases its toxicity very substantially. (p. 33)
Cannabis is also often combined with alcohol. Far from merely adding their respective effects, the resulting effect is much greater—what pharmacology calls potentiating synergy. (p. 59)
quote_texts.Q116:
General population surveys provide another measure of availability by asking people how easy they think it would be, or actually is, to obtain cannabis. They show that cannabis seems readily available to most French people, whether they use it or not: almost six in ten people aged 15 to 64 (58.0%) believe that, if they wanted it, obtaining cannabis within 24 hours would be easy (30.4% fairly easy and 27.5% very easy). Men aged 20–25 are particularly likely to hold this view (79.2%, compared with 61.3% in the rest of the population). Fewer than one person in ten (7.2%) says they cannot answer, a proportion that rises markedly with age, from 2.0% among 15–19-year-olds to 14.3% among those over 55. Admittedly, the question has limitations when put to people who have no desire to obtain cannabis and do not really accept the hypothetical situation presented to them.

Difficulties seem to have little effect on most users. Keeping small supplies in reserve, helping one another out and using alternative supply networks tend to cushion the impact of a temporary reduction in availability. An experienced regular user can obtain some form of cannabis to meet their needs in any circumstances.
quote_texts.Q117: Alcohol is responsible for the majority of fatal road accidents (around 30%); combined alcohol and cannabis use is also a factor (risk multiplied by fifteen, whereas cannabis alone does increase the risk, but by a factor of two—the same as alcohol at the permitted concentration of 0.5 g/L). (SAM study)
quote_texts.Q118:
At the beginning of the twenty-first century, the painkiller OxyContin is selling like hot cakes.

Prescribed for anything and everything, from the mildest headache to an inflamed knee, this “miracle” pill—normally intended for people with terminal cancer—is heavily marketed, and its use made to seem entirely routine.

And with good reason: its use rests on a misleading percentage, turned into a selling point by Purdue's sales representatives, who repeat it like a slogan:

“Fewer than 1% of patients who use OxyContin become addicted to it.”

A thoroughly false percentage, as hundreds of thousands of Americans soon become hooked on OxyContin, some to the point of taking excessive amounts.

The United States consequently sees a terrible rise in overdoses, under the indifferent gaze of a pharmaceutical company making a fortune.

That very company—one of the compelling features of Dopesick is that it reveals the plans of both Purdue's top executives and their critics—has only one thing in mind: exceeding a billion dollars in revenue, even if it means sacrificing its patients.
quote_texts.Q119: By decriminalising the use of all drugs twenty-five years ago, the country broke a taboo, and consumption remains contained at levels among the lowest in Europe.
quote_texts.Q120: We now know that while estimates vary, marijuana leads to dependence in around 9 to 10% of its adult users. By comparison, cocaine hooks 20% of those who use it. Around 25% of heroin users become addicted. The worst is tobacco, where the number is closer to 30% of smokers.
quote_texts.Q121: Cannabis use is most often temporary: even where dependence develops, two thirds of users stop using it spontaneously between the ages of 25 and 30.
quote_texts.Q122: One in three people who have tried cannabis becomes a regular user.
quote_texts.Q123: The addictive potential of cannabis is neither inherently low nor high, but depends on the level of use. There are no hard drugs and soft drugs, but hard or soft ways of using drugs, whatever they may be. Addiction lies in the relationship with the substance.
quote_texts.Q124: Legalisation would not cause consumption to soar if the tax set by the state kept the price at its current level (around €5.50 per gram). Price is the key variable: if it were too high, it would encourage trafficking. If it were too low, consumption could increase.
quote_texts.Q125: A US study by RAND Corporation economists published in 2010 estimated that legalising cannabis production and distribution in California could generate up to $1 billion in tax revenue, but would drive prices down by 80%, inevitably causing a substantial rise in consumption.
quote_texts.Q126: We relied on the fact that human rights conventions took legal precedence over drug conventions. Uruguay could therefore exercise its sovereignty by legalising cannabis if we demonstrated that doing so saved lives: those of young people risking their lives to obtain it on the black market, or of patients otherwise unable to relieve their pain.
quote_texts.Q127: Tobacco and alcohol are also appealing because many vested interests work to make them so.
quote_texts.Q128: A large meta-analysis in The Lancet examined alcohol consumption and its effects on the health of 28 million people between 1990 and 2016. Its conclusion: alcohol is harmful, even in small amounts.
quote_texts.Q129: The myth that a small daily glass protects your health has just been shattered. A large Brazilian study establishes a direct link between alcohol consumption, even in moderation, and the risk of dementia and Alzheimer's disease. More troubling still, the damage persists long after people stop drinking.
quote_texts.Q130: This overlooks the thirteen million people dependent on tobacco and the four or five million people dependent on alcohol who cannot go without a drink for even one day a week, drawn into using these two drugs by their legal status.
quote_texts.Q131: Continuing to use a substance despite knowing its harmful consequences is, in fact, part of the definition of addiction. Prohibition and punitive enforcement against use therefore cannot be enough to prevent psychoactive substance use, because users find these substances not only harmful but also appealing.
quote_texts.Q132: Six in ten French people believe that cannabis use could be permitted under certain conditions (adults only) and prohibited under others (before driving or for minors), compared with three in ten in 2008. However, a large majority of the population remains opposed to unrestricted cannabis sales (78%), although this proportion has fallen from the 85% who held that view in 2008.
quote_texts.Q133: 52% of French people believe that state-controlled cannabis sales would be more effective than prohibition at combating trafficking.
quote_texts.Q134: On alcohol, the state has abandoned, in the name of financial interests, the regulatory stance it appeared to adopt with the Évin Law, whose thirtieth anniversary we have celebrated.
quote_texts.Q135:
Investigators at the University of Connecticut produced a 60,000-page report identifying no fewer than 145 instances of fabricated or falsified data. This investigation completely discredits not only those fraudulent studies but also the others: why manipulate studies if wine's beneficial effects had really been proved? Might some scientists have taken bribes from wine-industry lobbyists? That appears to be the case.

A 60,000-page report is no small matter; one imagines there must have been a great deal to say.

The [http://tempsreel.nouvelobs.com/les-Internets-vous-parlent/20120116.OBS8929/le-vin-bon-pour-la-sante-des-etudes-etaient-bidonnees.html exposure] of this scientific fraud is far from an isolated case. It is much more widespread than we can imagine: scientists are, first and foremost, human beings, and therefore fallible and corruptible. Tell me who funds you, and I will tell you who you are.
quote_texts.Q136:
The government is going to shelve two alcohol-harm prevention campaigns that it had itself commissioned for the Rugby World Cup.

Apparently, the message “do not let alcohol knock you out” was too blunt for the alcohol industry's heavyweights. In the government's eyes, their economic weight matters far more than the public's health.

Clearly, alcohol is not the only thing that harms health: the alcohol industry's profits do too!
quote_texts.Q137: Between public health and the interests of wine-industry groups, the members of parliament seeking to amend the Évin Law have made their choice. They have chosen to defend wine-industry lobbyists, knowing full well that their vote threatened the community's health interests.
quote_texts.Q138: Those of our partners who thought they were doing the right thing by relaxing cannabis legislation are reversing course! In the United Kingdom, the Labour government returned cannabis to the category of dangerous drugs four years after downgrading it. As for the Netherlands, that emblem of the so-called “tolerance” policy, it is changing its approach: sharply restricting access to coffee shops, now closed to non-residents, and gradually erasing the distinction between hard and soft drugs…
quote_texts.Q139: As with any product, even water, the danger lies in excess, and excessive use should be avoided whether it begins early or not. Water can kill if consumed to excess. Cannabis can have a harmful effect on life if used to excess, even occasionally for fun. But this applies to everything: coffee (nervousness, insomnia and addiction), chocolate (indigestion and addiction), potatoes, cheese, cigars and so on. Cannabis use by people whose brains are not fully developed is controversial, and no tangible evidence has yet established that this argument is valid.
quote_texts.Q140: The adolescent brain is more vulnerable to psychoactive substances than the adult brain. It is in a transitional state on the way to adulthood. Brain maturation processes, which continue until around the age of 25, make adolescents particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxicity of psychoactive substances in general. One area, the prefrontal cortex, which enables decision-making and the adaptation of behaviour to circumstances, is particularly affected by this maturation during adolescence.
quote_texts.Q141:
Fear of punishment deters only those who are already least likely to use drugs and who do not have problematic patterns of use.

According to the EMCDDA's 2011 report, there is no correlation between the level of punitive enforcement and declining use. Conversely, decriminalisation does not lead to a significant increase in cannabis consumption.
quote_texts.Q142: Most young people smoke it anyway; if all we do is punish them, trafficking will continue.
quote_texts.Q143: Of around forty studies analysed by California statistician Meenakshi Sabina Subbaraman, sixteen conclude that alcohol and cannabis are substitutes, while ten conclude that they are instead consumed as complements.
quote_texts.Q144: These same advocates of cannabis decriminalisation are often also campaigning for the decriminalisation of every other drug. As a first crowning achievement of their efforts to recruit addicts indiscriminately, they argued for the introduction of drug injection rooms and have just secured the ministry's approval for them.
quote_texts.Q145:
N. M. — If we legalise cannabis, it becomes a market product. A commercial company seeks to sell it. It wants market share. That is inevitable.

M. H. — Unless we establish a state monopoly or state control.

N. M. — I do not see how cannabis production and sales could become a state monopoly when the European Union requires us to end all protectionist policies.
quote_texts.Q146: We need to draw on users' expertise. We should take more interest in the person than in the substance. Cannabis is emblematic in this respect: a so-called soft drug that can be used in hard ways. The reverse can also be true: so-called hard substances can be used in soft ways. Use must therefore be placed at the centre of policy. In France, however, all we promote for cannabis is abstinence.
quote_texts.Q147: Legalising the market for certain forms of cannabis could also help create a parallel market selling more potent cannabis with stronger effects, which is also something consumers seek.
quote_texts.Q148: The cannabis black market still accounts for 80% of sales in places that have legalised it, such as California.
quote_texts.Q149:
Prohibition laws have made the illicit drug trade a thriving international market.
These sellers operate in ways that meet the same needs as any legal market: identifying potential customers, ensuring repeat business, attracting new customers and so on. But since the trade, potency and quality of the products are unregulated, anything goes when it comes to expanding that market, whether selling drugs to children or introducing extremely toxic products. Some sellers aim to create lifelong customers by encouraging patterns of consumption more likely to cause dependence than other, safer ways of using drugs. Products also change over time to maintain customers' interest, creating trends and regularly bringing new products onto the market […]. Sellers also try to reach the widest possible customer base by offering drugs across a broad price range […]. Similarly, they seek to expand the market geographically by dumping drugs in previously little-affected areas to attract new customers. This situation should come as no surprise. The illicit drug market is a highly profitable global market. It is worth sellers' while to use the best possible techniques to distribute and promote their products.

'''Legalisation''' permits previously prohibited activities within a defined framework, whether production, distribution, sale or use. It does not necessarily mean unrestricted or unregulated sales. Restrictions on age, advertising, quality and quantity may vary.

Portugal's reform, which came into force in 2001, decriminalised drug use, acquisition and possession for personal use under the conditions set out in the law. It did not legalise trafficking or establish a legal commercial drug market<ref>[https://www.euda.europa.eu/system/files/media/publications/documents/11331/portugal-cdr-2019.pdf EMCDDA, Portugal — Country Drug Report 2019, “National drug laws”].</ref>.

subsections.title: The legal position in France
subsections.content:
Unlawful use of controlled drugs remains a criminal offence in France. The Service Public information page reviewed on 21 August 2026 states that use carries a maximum penalty of one year's imprisonment and a €3,750 fine. Offences relating to supply, trafficking, cultivation or driving after drug use must be distinguished: this maximum cannot be applied indiscriminately to all of them<ref name="sp-usage-2026">[https://www.service-public.gouv.fr/particuliers/vosdroits/F33341 Que risque-t-on pour usage de drogues ?], Service Public / DILA, information page reviewed on 21 August 2026.</ref>.

'''A fixed fine does not mean decriminalisation of use'''

According to the same dated page, the fixed fine is €500, reduced to €400 if paid within fifteen days and increased to €1,000 after forty-five days. This procedure does not make drug use legal and is not the same as reclassifying the offence as a ''contravention''. The amounts and conditions must be checked against the law in force for the period concerned<ref name="sp-usage-2026" />.

<references />

subsections.title: Comparing experience in other countries
subsections.content:
Canada opened a legal market for non-medical cannabis in 2018. Its expert panel reported progress in 2024 in regulated supply and the shift in demand towards the legal market, alongside persistent problems, particularly protecting young people and addressing high-THC products<ref>[https://www.canada.ca/fr/sante-canada/services/publications/drogues-medicaments/examen-legislatif-loi-cannabis-rapport-final-comite-experts.html Examen législatif de la Loi sur le cannabis : Rapport final du Comité d’experts], Health Canada, 2024.</ref>.

Portugal's approach is one of decriminalisation and should not be equated with this form of legalisation. In each country, rules on use, the organisation of supply, health indicators and the role of the illicit market need to be considered separately.
<references />

introduction_version_2.adaptation_note_fr: Le centrage français est explicité pour le lectorat anglophone. Les distinctions délit/contravention, dépénalisation/légalisation et les réserves temporelles sont conservées. Les montants et dates sont traduits fidèlement depuis la source, sans prétendre à une vérification juridique actuelle. L'image française n'est pas transposée vers un fichier anglais dont l'existence n'a pas été vérifiée. Les références françaises des sous-parties restent identifiées comme sources françaises dans ce brouillon documentaire. La première sous-partie, non titrée dans la source, reçoit le titre fonctionnel « The question » pour respecter le modèle Subsection sans créer de contenu supplémentaire.
